prompt: In a Bubble Tea program, what is allowed to change the model?
hint: One of the three methods returns a model.

choices.text: Only `Update`, by returning the next model
choices.why: Right. The program keeps whatever `Update` returns, and nothing else in the loop produces a model.

choices.text: `View`, when what it draws needs a field corrected
choices.why: `View` only reads the model and returns a `tea.View`. A change made inside it would be made to a copy and thrown away.

choices.text: The key press itself, before any method runs
choices.why: A key press becomes a message. It changes nothing until `Update` decides what the next model is.

choices.text: `Init`, which Bubble Tea calls again before each frame
choices.why: `Init` runs once, before the first screen, and returns a command rather than a model.

prompt: A colleague's `View` opens the log and counts it again every time it is called, so that the numbers are always fresh. What goes wrong?
hint: How often does the loop call `View`?

choices.text: Bubble Tea refuses to compile a `View` that does I/O
choices.why: Nothing in the type system stops it; `View` is an ordinary method. The trouble shows up at run time.

choices.text: Nothing: `View` runs only once, when the program starts
choices.why: `View` runs after every `Update`, which means after every key press and every other message.

choices.text: Every key press rereads the whole file before the screen moves
choices.why: Right. `View` runs after every `Update`, so each message pays for a full count and the keys queue up behind it. The reading belongs in a command.

choices.text: The counts go stale, because Bubble Tea caches the first `View`
choices.why: There is no such cache; every `View` result is drawn. The cost is the opposite one: far too much work.

prompt: Match each piece of a Bubble Tea program with when it runs.
hint: One of the right-hand phrases describes nothing in the loop.

pairs.right: for every message, one at a time
in a goroutine of its own

right_distractors: only when the terminal is resized

prompt: Code from an older tutorial declares `func (m model) View() string` and starts with `tea.NewProgram(m, tea.WithAltScreen())`. Against `charm.land/bubbletea/v2` it does not compile. What is the version 2 shape?
hint: In version 2 the view says what the terminal should be doing.

choices.text: `View` returns a `tea.View`, and setting its `AltScreen` field asks for the alternate screen
choices.why: Right. Version 2 made the view declarative: `tea.NewView(s)` wraps the text, and `v.AltScreen = true` replaces the program option.

choices.text: Keep `View() string` and call `tea.EnterAltScreen` from `Init`
choices.why: `tea.EnterAltScreen` is one of the commands version 2 removed, and `View` no longer returns a string.

choices.text: Change only the import path; the rest is the same API
choices.why: The import path changed and so did the API: the type `View` returns and the way the alternate screen is asked for.

choices.text: Return the text from `Update` and drop `View`
choices.why: `View` is one of the three methods of `tea.Model`. A type without it is not a model at all.

prompt: A Bubble Tea program whose `Update` has no `"ctrl+c"` case cannot be stopped with Ctrl+C. Why not?
hint: What mode does Bubble Tea put the terminal in?

choices.text: Go programs ignore `SIGINT` unless they call `signal.Notify`
choices.why: Without `signal.Notify`, `SIGINT` kills a Go program. Here no signal is sent at all.

choices.text: In raw mode the keystroke arrives as a key message, not as a signal
choices.why: Right. The terminal driver stops turning Ctrl+C into `SIGINT`, so the program sees `"ctrl+c"` like any key and must handle it.

choices.text: The alternate screen captures Ctrl+C and discards it
choices.why: The alternate screen is a second buffer to draw on; it has nothing to do with how keys are delivered.

choices.text: Ctrl+C reaches `View`, which has no way to quit
choices.why: Every message goes to `Update`; `View` receives none.

prompt: In Bubble Tea version 2, pressing a key delivers a message of type `tea.___`; `tea.KeyMsg` is now an interface that also covers releases.
hint: Its name says the key went down.

prompt: In `hits browse`, what does the breakdown screen draw if Enter is handled before the first `tea.WindowSizeMsg` has arrived?
hint: What is `width` in a freshly built model?

choices.text: The counts, with no bars
choices.why: Right. `width` is 0 until the first `WindowSizeMsg`, `bar` gets a negative width and returns an empty string, and the counts are drawn alone.

choices.text: Bars sized for an 80-column terminal, the usual default
choices.why: The model has no default of its own; it knows only what the messages told it, and nothing has told it a width yet.

choices.text: Nothing: `Update` ignores Enter until it knows the size
choices.why: The Enter case checks only that there are rows. The width matters to `View`, not to `Update`.

choices.text: It panics, because `strings.Repeat` is given a count below zero
choices.why: `bar` returns early when the width is below 1, so `strings.Repeat` never sees a negative count.

prompt: On a terminal 72 columns wide, the breakdown of `/static/app.js` drew 56 `#` for its largest count, 944, and 20 for `404`'s 340. With integer division as `bar` does it, how many `#` would `404` get on a terminal 100 columns wide?
hint: The bar has width − 16 columns; it is n × that ÷ the largest count, rounded down.

prompt: `hits browse` reads the log in a command returned by `Init` instead of reading it inside `Init`. What does that buy?
hint: Where does the program run a command?

choices.text: The screen answers keys while the file is read
choices.why: Right. The program runs a command in a goroutine of its own, so the first screen is drawn at once; the result arrives later as `loaded`. A blocking read in `Init` would hold up that screen.

choices.text: The file is read twice as fast
choices.why: The reading loop is the same either way; what changes is which goroutine waits for it.

choices.text: `Init` is not allowed to open files
choices.why: `Init` is an ordinary method and may do anything; doing slow work there is the problem.

choices.text: A command can change the model directly, which `Init` cannot
choices.why: A command never touches the model. It returns a message, and `Update` makes the change.

prompt: What is `tea.Quit`, which `Update` returns when `q` is pressed?

choices.text: A function that calls `os.Exit(0)` straight away
choices.why: Nothing exits on the spot. The program finishes its loop and `Run` returns, which is what lets `browse` print an error afterwards.

choices.text: A command: a `func() tea.Msg` that returns `tea.QuitMsg`
choices.why: Right. It has exactly the type of a `tea.Cmd`, and when its message comes round the loop the program stops.

choices.text: A field of the model that `View` checks
choices.why: The model is the program's own type; Bubble Tea adds no fields to it.

choices.text: The signal Bubble Tea sends itself on Ctrl+C
choices.why: In raw mode Ctrl+C is a key message; `tea.Quit` is returned by the program's own `Update`.

prompt: Put in order what happens when `./hits browse bad.log` runs on a terminal and line 1 of `bad.log` will not parse.
hint: The message is printed last, for a reason.
items: the command `Init` returned runs `count` in its own goroutine
`count` returns `loaded` carrying the error for line 1
`Update` keeps the error in the model and returns `tea.Quit`
the alternate screen is switched off and `Run` returns
`browse` prints `hits: line 1: want 5 fields, got 1` and returns 1

prompt: `HITS_DEBUG=msgs.log` recorded every message of one run. Which of these came from Bubble Tea or the terminal, rather than from the person typing or from `hits`'s own code? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them nobody asked for.

choices.text: `tea.ColorProfileMsg`
choices.why: Right. Bubble Tea tells the model how many colours the terminal can show.

choices.text: `tui.loaded`
choices.why: That is `hits`'s own message, returned by the command `Init` started.

choices.text: `tea.ModeReportMsg`
choices.why: Right. These were the terminal's answers to Bubble Tea's questions about modes 2026 and 2027.

choices.text: `tea.KeyPressMsg`
choices.why: Those were `j`, `j` and `q`, typed by the person at the keyboard.

choices.text: `tea.EnvMsg`
choices.why: Right. Bubble Tea hands the model the environment it was started with.

prompt: `TestScreens` compares the whole string `View` returned with the screen it expects, instead of checking that the text contains `/login`. What failure would the shorter check miss?
hint: Two rows of the list both contain a path.

choices.text: A `View` that panics on an empty log
choices.why: That is a different input altogether; `TestEmptyLog` is the test that feeds an empty log.

choices.text: A count that took too long to finish
choices.why: The test runs the command synchronously; time is not what either check measures.

choices.text: The `>` beside the wrong row
choices.why: Right. `/login` is on the screen wherever the cursor is; only the whole string pins down which row carries the `>`.

choices.text: Escape sequences that the terminal would not understand
choices.why: `View().Content` is the text before Bubble Tea turns it into escape sequences, so neither check sees them.

prompt: Why does `browse` use `term.IsTerminal` rather than checking `os.Stdout.Stat()` for `os.ModeCharDevice`?
hint: Run `stat -c %F` on the file a script uses to throw output away.

choices.text: `ModeCharDevice` is only defined on Windows
choices.why: It is defined on every platform; the stat in the section ran on Linux.

choices.text: `/dev/null` is a character device too, so the shorter test would start a screen nobody sees
choices.why: Right. `stat` reported `character special file` for `/dev/null`; `term.IsTerminal` asks whether the descriptor is a terminal, and refuses it.

choices.text: `Stat` on standard output fails while a terminal is attached
choices.why: `Stat` works on any open descriptor. The problem is what it cannot tell apart.

choices.text: Bubble Tea requires `golang.org/x/term`
choices.why: Bubble Tea brings its own terminal package; `hits` imports `golang.org/x/term` for its own check.

prompt: With its terminal check deleted, `./hits-raw browse access.log > screen.out` left 108 bytes in the file. What were they?

choices.text: The list of paths, without colours
choices.why: Not one path reached the file: `grep` counted no line with `login` in it.

choices.text: An error message saying there was no terminal
choices.why: Bubble Tea does not refuse when its output is not a terminal; it starts anyway, which is why the check exists.

choices.text: Escape sequences, and no data at all
choices.why: Right. `od -c` shows `033 [ ? 2 0 2 6 $ p` and similar: questions and mode switches meant for a terminal, written into a file.

choices.text: The `msgs.log` debug lines
choices.why: Those go to the file named by `HITS_DEBUG`, and only when it is set.

prompt: A teammate wants a cron job that emails the busiest path of the day every morning, and proposes running `hits browse` with its output captured. What do you tell them?
hint: What is standard output in a cron job?

choices.text: Use `hits top -n 1`: `browse` refuses without a terminal
choices.why: Right. Cron gives the job no terminal, so `browse` stops with status 2; `top` prints a line of data and an exit code, which is what a job can use.

choices.text: Fine, as long as they send `q` on standard input
choices.why: The check runs before any key is read: with no terminal on standard output, `browse` stops at once with status 2.

choices.text: Fine, but strip the colours with `sed` first
choices.why: There are no colours to strip and no data either: `browse` refuses, and without the check the file would hold only escape sequences.

choices.text: Run it with `HITS_DEBUG` set and parse the log of messages
choices.why: The debug log is for watching the program; the terminal check still refuses before anything runs.

prompt: You add an `r` key to `hits browse` that reads the log again. Where does the reading go?
hint: Section 04 says how a model asks for work.

choices.text: In `Update`, which reads the file and stores the new rows before returning
choices.why: That blocks the loop: no `View`, no keys, until the read is done. It is the mistake section 04 opens with.

choices.text: In `Update` on `r`, returning a command that counts and sends `loaded`
choices.why: Right. The case returns `m, count(...)`; the result arrives as a message like the first one, and the existing `loaded` case takes it.

choices.text: In `View`, so that the rows are fresh whenever the screen is drawn
choices.why: `View` runs after every message, and a model it changed would be a copy nobody keeps.

choices.text: In a goroutine started from `Update` that writes `m.rows` when done
choices.why: `m` is a copy that has already been returned, so the rows land in a model nobody keeps and the screen never changes.

prompt: A Bubble Tea command has the type `func() tea.___`: it does its work and hands back a value for `Update`.
hint: The same type every message satisfies.

prompt: Lesson 1's standard-library `hits` was 4,031,903 bytes; with `browse`, Bubble Tea and `golang.org/x/term` it is 6,773,596 bytes. By what percentage did the binary grow, to the nearest whole number?
